q: my 18 month old has a fever of 103 and won't take Tylenol
text:
103 °F = 39.4 °C.

A fever is usually a sign the body is fighting an infection, and most children get better within a few days [1][5]. The goal is your child's comfort, not bringing the number down to normal [3].

If she won't take Tylenol, you can try acetaminophen or ibuprofen — both reduce fever in children [4]. Give acetaminophen every 4 to 6 hours, or ibuprofen every 6 to 8 hours; know her weight before dosing [4]. Don't give ibuprofen if she is under 6 months, and never give aspirin to a child [4]. Offer plenty of fluids in small sips, keep the room comfortably cool, and don't bundle her up [3]. Don't force food — it's normal for her not to want to eat [3]. Don't use cold baths or wet cloths; they're unpleasant and don't help [3].

Get help if:
- Fever lasts more than 1 to 4 days [5]
- She has a seizure [5]
- She seems very unwell, won't drink, or has fewer wet nappies [3]

q: can I give him both Tylenol and Motrin at the same time
text:
No, do not give ibuprofen and paracetamol at the same time, according to the NHS [2]. If paracetamol is not helping, you can try ibuprofen instead if it is suitable for your child [2]. You can alternate between them only if a doctor or nurse tells you to, and it helps to write down when you gave each medicine so the doses are spaced evenly [2].

Ibuprofen is not for children under 6 months [1], and it should not be given if your child has asthma, chickenpox or is dehydrated [6]. Acetaminophen can be given every 4 to 6 hours, and ibuprofen every 6 to 8 hours [1]. Know your child's weight before giving either medicine [1].

q: my 4 year old has a rash on her stomach and chest after fever went away
text:
A rash on the chest and stomach after a fever has gone is a pattern doctors look at closely, and the SEUP lists "spots on the skin that fade when pressed" among the reasons to go to the emergency department [3]. Spots that do **not** fade when pressed are the ones to worry about.

What to do now: keep her comfortable and offer fluids often in small amounts. Do not give ibuprofen if she has spots that do not fade when pressed or any bleeding.

Get help if:
- Spots that do not fade when pressed [3]
- Fever above 38°C (100.4 °F) lasting more than 5 days [3]
- Vomiting or diarrhoea with any warning sign [3]
- Trouble breathing [5]
- Fever with any skin, behaviour or breathing warning sign [5]

If she is drinking, alert and the rash fades when pressed, ask your doctor to see her to check what is causing it.

q: my baby fell off the bed and bumped his head (age: 8 months) (weight: 18 lbs)
text:
18 lb = 8.2 kg.

A bump on the head is a common injury in babies, and most head injuries are mild because the skull protects the brain, according to MedlinePlus [2]. The SEUP says most children recover quickly, though some may have symptoms for several hours or even days [6].

What to do now: you can let him sleep, but after a more significant knock it is advisable to wake him every 4 hours [6]. He can keep to his usual feeding according to his appetite — no special diet is needed [6]. If he has a headache, you can give paracetamol or ibuprofen in the dose your doctor indicates [6]. Keep him resting, without sports or screens, for 24 to 48 hours depending on how hard the knock was [4].

Get help if:
- A headache that gets worse or does not go away [2]
- Repeated vomiting or nausea [2]
- Hard to wake, or very irritable [4]
- Confusion, or trouble speaking or walking [4]
- Blood or clear fluid from the nose or ears [4]
- A seizure, or weakness in the arms or legs [2]

q: why does my 3 year old have a temperature of 105 degree celsius
text:
105 °F = 40.6 °C.

A temperature of 105 °F (about 40.5 °C (104.9 °F)) is a high fever, and fever itself is not an illness — it is usually a sign the body is fighting an infection, according to MedlinePlus [1]. Most fevers in children are harmless and self-limited, and fever rarely goes above 40.5 °C (104.9 °F) on its own [5].

What to do now: check the temperature with a thermometer, and if there are no warning signs, start with physical measures — take off extra clothing, offer fluids, reduce activity, and a lukewarm bath only if the child is comfortable [5]. If the child is uncomfortable, paracetamol or ibuprofen can be given; paracetamol is the first choice [4]. The dose depends on the child's weight — you can use PediBot's dose calculator for paracetamol or ibuprofen.

Get help if:
- The child is very sleepy, confused, irritable or behaving abnormally [6]
- Severe headache or repeated vomiting [6]
- A seizure (convulsion) [6]
- Fever lasts or the child seems to get worse

Fever is not the danger by itself — how the child looks and acts matters most [5].

q: she ate a small coin about an hour ago but she is breathing fine
text:
A swallowed coin is a choking risk because small objects like coins can block the airway, according to MedlinePlus [3]. Since she is breathing fine, the coin has not blocked her airway — but a swallowed object still needs medical assessment.

Do not try to make her vomit, and do not give her water, milk, oil or any food, according to the SEUP [2]. If you can see something solid in her mouth and can reach it safely, remove it — never blindly, as that could make things worse [2]. Try to work out what and how much she swallowed [2].

Get medical help now: a swallowed object, especially batteries or magnets, is a reason to go to the emergency department [6]. Also go if she stops responding normally, breathes badly or changes colour [2], or if she develops trouble breathing, chest pain, or becomes drowsy or very irritable [5].

q: how to introduce peanut butter to 6 month old
text:
Peanut butter can be introduced from around 6 months, just like any other food, according to the NHS [1]. Give it one new food at a time so you can spot any reaction [1]. Serve peanuts finely ground or as nut butter — never whole nuts, which are a choking risk for a baby this age [1].

Offer a small amount of smooth peanut butter thinned into their usual food, then wait and watch. If it is tolerated, keep it in their regular diet; delaying peanut beyond 6 to 12 months may raise the risk of allergy [1]. If your baby has a diagnosed food allergy or eczema, or there is a family history of allergy, eczema, asthma or hay fever, talk to your doctor before introducing it [1].

Signs of a food allergy usually start within minutes to two hours and can include:

- Hives or red, itchy skin [3]
- Swelling of the face, lips or tongue [3]
- Vomiting or diarrhoea [3]
- Coughing or wheezing [3]
- Trouble breathing, dizziness or fainting — this is an emergency [3]

[3] MedlinePlus — "Alergia a los alimentos", section "¿Cuáles son los síntomas de las aler

q: my 5 year old won't stop itching her arms and legs at night
text:
Itching that is worse at night is a common pattern in scabies, which is an itchy rash caused by mites and spreads through close skin contact [5]. Scabies symptoms usually begin 4–6 weeks after infestation and include severe itch, often worse at night, with itchy lines and bumps on the fingers, wrists, arms and legs [2]. It should be treated quickly to stop it spreading [5].

See your doctor so it can be checked and treated properly. Until then, keep your child's fingernails cut short and put socks on their hands at night to stop scratching, bathe in cool water and pat the skin dry without rubbing, dress them in loose clothes, and ask a pharmacist about antihistamine medicine to help the itching [3].

Get help if:
- The itch is severe or keeps your child awake [2]
- Sores fill with pus, break open or form a thick crust [1]
- Scratching leads to skin sores or infection [2]

q: how long does flu last in toddlers
text:
Most children get better from flu on their own, and it usually passes in about a week [6]. The cough can linger longer than the fever [5].

While your toddler is ill, keep them at home so they don't pass it on, let them rest, and offer plenty of fluids [3]. Treat other symptoms, like fever, as you normally would [3]. If they seem uncomfortable with a fever above 38ºC (100.4 °F), you can give the usual anti-fever medicine your paediatrician recommends [5].

Get medical help if their symptoms get worse [3]. Children under five are among those at higher risk of complications, so it is worth asking your doctor early on [6].

q: can my 10 year old take adult Tylenol if I cut it in half
text:
No, do not give your 10-year-old a cut-in-half adult Tylenol. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) helps reduce fever in children and adults, according to MedlinePlus, but the amount you give depends on your child's weight, so you need to know how much they weigh before giving it [1]. Adult tablets are made for adult weights, and cutting one in half does not give a safe or accurate child's dose.

Instead, use a children's acetaminophen product and give the dose based on your child's weight, following the packet or leaflet that comes with the medicine [1][3]. Acetaminophen is usually given every 4 to 6 hours [1]. If you are not sure whether your child should take it, or how much, speak to a pharmacist or doctor [3].

Get medical advice if you have given your child more than the packet, leaflet or prescription says, because too much paracetamol can sometimes be dangerous [6].

q: my 14 year old says her throat hurts really bad when swallowing
text:
A sore throat that hurts when swallowing is usually caused by a virus, like a cold or flu, and normally gets better by itself within a week, according to the NHS [4][5]. It can also be tonsillitis, which is common in teenagers and causes a sore throat and problems swallowing [2].

To help soothe it: drink plenty of water, eat cool or soft foods, suck ice cubes, ice lollies or hard sweets, rest, and avoid smoking or smoky places [5]. She is old enough to gargle with warm, salty water — half a teaspoon of salt in a glass of warm water, then spit it out, not swallow [5].

See a doctor if:
- The sore throat does not improve after a week [7]
- A very high temperature, or feeling hot, cold or shivery [7]
- Signs of dehydration, such as peeing less than usual or dark, strong-smelling pee [7]
- A lump in the mouth or neck, or a mouth ulcer lasting more than 3 weeks [7]

Get help now if she has difficulty breathing or cannot swallow, is drooling, or makes a high-pitched sound when breathing [7].

A fever is usually a sign that your body is fighting an infection, and most infections that cause it are mild and get better on their own, according to the SEUP [3]. Chills and sweating often come along with it [4].

q: is the MMR vaccine safe for my baby I read online it causes autism
text:
The MMR vaccine is safe, and there is no link between it and autism. Studies have found no evidence that the MMR vaccine causes autism, according to the NHS [1]. Many scientific studies have looked at this and found no link between vaccines and autism, according to MedlinePlus [5].

The American Academy of Pediatrics, the National Academy of Medicine, and the CDC have all concluded that the benefits of vaccines outweigh their risks [3]. Children need 2 doses of MMR vaccine, usually the first at age 12 through 15 months and the second at age 4 through 6 years, following the United States schedule [6]. It can be given at the same time as other vaccines [6].

Serious allergic reactions are rare and usually happen within minutes, when the person who vaccinates your child is trained to treat them immediately [7].

Talk to your doctor if you are worried about your child having a vaccine or are not sure whether they can have it [7].

q: what are the side effects of chickenpox shot
text:
Most side effects of the chickenpox vaccine are mild and do not last long, according to the NHS. They can include pain or swelling where the injection was given, a high temperature, and a rash either at the injection site or more widespread, usually within 1 month of vaccination [1].

Serious side effects, such as a severe allergic reaction, are very rare, and the person who gives the vaccine is trained to treat them immediately [1].

If the vaccine is given as part of the combined MMRV vaccine, common side effects are usually mild and last 2 to 3 days: a raised, blotchy rash, feeling unwell, and a high temperature about 6 to 10 days afterwards; swelling around the face and aching joints about 2 to 3 weeks afterwards; and a spotty rash at the injection site about 3 to 4 weeks afterwards [2]. That spotty rash may contain infectious chickenpox virus and should be covered with clothes; as long as the spots are covered, children can go to nursery as normal [2].

Get help if:
- Difficulty breathing, swelling of the face or throat, fast heartbeat, dizziness or weakness [3]
- A severe allergic reaction can sometimes start after leaving the clinic [3]

q: can I give Nurofen as well
text: Yes, you can give ibuprofen (Nurofen) instead of paracetamol if the paracetamol is not helping, according to the NHS [1]. q: my 4 year old has red spots all over his back and he is scratching them
text:
A rash that is very itchy and turns into fluid-filled blisters that then crust over is the typical picture of chickenpox, which is usually mild and lasts 5 to 10 days, according to MedlinePlus [4]. It often starts on the face, chest and back before spreading [4].

To help at home: cut your child's fingernails and put socks on their hands at night to stop scratching, use cooling creams or gels, ask a pharmacist about antihistamine medicine for the itching, bathe in cool water and pat the skin dry without rubbing, and dress them in loose clothes, according to the NHS [1]. Calamine creams and oatmeal baths can also help the itch [4]. Give paracetamol for pain or discomfort [1]. Do not use ibuprofen unless a doctor tells you to, as it may cause serious skin infections, and do not give aspirin to children under 16 [1].

Keep them away from newborn babies, anyone pregnant, and anyone with a weakened immune system [1].

Get help if:
- They seem very unwell or you are worried [1]
- The spots become very painful, hot or swollen [1]
- They are not drinking or are dehydrated [1]

q: when should I start giving finger foods to my 6 month old
text:
Around 6 months is the right time to start, according to the WHO: by then your baby's energy and nutrient needs begin to exceed what breast milk alone provides, and complementary foods are needed to cover them [3]. Starting too early or too late can affect growth [3].

Begin with small amounts and increase them gradually as your baby grows, and build up the consistency and variety of foods over time [3]. Aim for 2–3 meals a day at 6 to 8 months, plus 1–2 snacks if needed [3]. Keep breastfeeding on demand alongside the food [3].

Finger foods are one option: some parents let their baby feed themselves from the start, others combine this with spoon-feeding, and there is no right or wrong way — what matters is that your baby eats a wide variety of food and gets the nutrients they need [1]. The risk of choking is no greater when a baby feeds themselves than when fed with a spoon [1].

q: my 5 year old complains of stomach ache and won't eat anything

- is refusing food markedly [7]

q: my 8 year old has a sore throat and high temp
text:
A sore throat with a high temperature is common in children and is usually caused by a virus, according to the NHS [1][4]. It normally gets better by itself within a week [5].

To help now: offer plenty of water and cool or soft foods, and let them rest [5]. Avoid smoky places [5]. For pain or fever, an over-the-counter pain reliever can help, but do not give aspirin to a child [6] — paracetamol or ibuprofen at the dose for their weight is what the NHS advises for children's fever, and PediBot's dose calculator can work that out.

- Very high temperature, or hot, cold or shivery [2]
- Signs of dehydration — peeing less, or dark strong-smelling pee [2]
- Not improving after a week [2]
- Difficulty breathing or unable to swallow [2]
- Drooling, or a high-pitched sound when breathing [2]

q: is MMR jab safe for my daughter
text:
The MMR vaccine is safe and is the best protection against measles, mumps and rubella, according to the NHS [3]. Protection starts within 2 weeks of the jab, and after 2 doses around 99% of people are protected against measles and rubella and around 88% against mumps [3]. If your daughter does get mumps after being vaccinated, the symptoms are usually much milder [3].

In the UK, the MMR vaccine is offered as part of the national schedule, with doses in early childhood and a booster before school age [1]. If she has missed a dose, contact your GP to catch up — it is important vaccines are given on time for the best protection [1].

If you have any questions about whether the vaccine is right for your daughter, speak to your GP or practice nurse.

Chickenpox usually lasts about 4 to 7 days, according to the CDC [1]. Most children miss 5 to 6 days of school or childcare because of it [1].

q: my 1 year old has a terrible nappy rash with red dots
text:
Nappy rash is common in babies and can usually be treated at home, according to the NHS [1]. It often includes red or raw patches on the bottom or the whole nappy area, and spots, pimples or blisters that can look red or brown [1][2]. It can happen when skin stays in contact with pee or poo, when nappies are not changed often enough, from rubbing, from fragranced or alcohol wipes, or from thrush [6].

Change the nappy often and clean the area gently [6]. A pharmacist can recommend a nappy rash cream or medicine, and may suggest a thin layer of barrier cream at each nappy change [4][5].

See your doctor if your baby is in a lot of discomfort or they think there might be an infection — they may prescribe a steroid cream, an antifungal cream for thrush, or antibiotics for a bacterial infection [3].

q: my 6 year old has a barking cough at night
text:
A barking cough that comes on at night, often after a few days of cold-like symptoms, is typical of croup — an inflammation of the voice box and windpipe that is usually caused by a virus, according to MedlinePlus [2]. Most cases are mild and can be treated at home [2], and symptoms usually settle within a few days, though they can last up to a week, according to the SEUP [4].

Offer fluids if there is a fever and give the usual fever medicine [4]. Keep your child calm — crying and getting upset can make the noise worse [3]. Do not put your child in a steamy room or have them breathe in steam [7]. Do not give cough syrups or cough suppositories without checking with your paediatrician [5].

Get help if:
- Noisy breathing when breathing in, even at rest [5]
- Breathing gets faster, ribs pull in, or chest sucks in [5]
- Trouble swallowing or lots of drooling [5]
- Struggling to breathe, or blue, grey or pale skin, lips or tongue [7]
- Sleepier than normal, difficult to wake, or floppy [7]

q: my 3 year old baby has 101 fever and cold
text:
101 °F = 38.3 °C.

A temperature of 101°F is a fever, and fever is the body's normal response to fighting an infection like a cough or cold, according to the NHS [1]. It is not an illness in itself and is usually not a reason to worry [6].

What to do now: check the temperature with a thermometer, under the arm is fine [6]. If your child has no warning signs, start with physical measures — take off extra clothing, offer fluids, reduce activity, and a lukewarm bath only if your child is comfortable [6]. You do not always need medicine: the aim is to relieve discomfort, not to remove all fever [6]. If you do give paracetamol or ibuprofen, the dose depends on your child's weight — use PediBot's dose calculator. Do not give aspirin to a child under 16 [1]. Do not alternate ibuprofen and paracetamol unless a doctor or nurse tells you to [1]. Do not undress or sponge your child to cool them, and do not cover them in too many clothes [1].

Get help if your child:
- has a rash that does not fade when pressed [1]
- has a stiff neck, is bothered by light, or has a first fit [1]
- is drowsy and hard to wake, or confused [1]
- has difficulty breathing or is breathing very fast [1]
- has a fever lasting 5 days or more [1]

q: my 4 year old has loose motion 5 times since morning
text:
Loose, watery stools five times in a day is diarrhoea, and gastroenteritis is usually not serious, according to MedlinePlus [2]. The main risk to watch for is dehydration [4].

Keep giving your child fluids. Oral rehydration solution (a mix of clean water, salt and sugar) is what the WHO recommends for diarrhoea [5]. Offer it in small amounts often, and keep offering it as long as the loose stools continue [3]. Do not use homemade solutions or fizzy drinks to replace the losses [3]. Do not give medicines for the diarrhoea or vomiting without asking your paediatrician [3].

Get help if your child has:
- Diarrhoea lasting more than a day [2]
- Frequent loose stools or vomiting often [2]
- Signs of dehydration: thirst, dry mouth, urinating less than usual, no wet nappies for 3 hours or more, no tears when crying [2]
- Severe belly or rectal pain [2]
- Stools that are black and tarry, or contain blood or pus [2]

text:
Vomiting after eating is common in young children and is often caused by a gut infection, and the main risk to watch for is dehydration, according to the SEUP [5].

q: how to start cerelac for 5 month baby
text:
At 5 months, the AEP recommends waiting until 6 months to start complementary feeding in breastfed babies, and never before 4 months in any baby [4]. Starting too early can raise the risk of choking and of infections such as gastroenteritis and upper respiratory infections [4].

When the time comes, cereals can be offered in many forms — powder dissolved in milk, added to purées, or as boiled and mashed rice, bread, pasta, corn cakes, quinoa or oats — depending on the baby's age, stage of development and family customs [6]. If you express milk, cereal powder can be added to it for one of the feeds, but do not replace a breastfeed with formula just to give cereals [6]. Choose cereals without honey or added sugars [6].

Signs the baby is ready to start other foods depend on their motor development, and not all children gain these skills at the same age [1].

q: my 2 year old has bad cough at night not sleeping
text:
A cough that is worse at night and stops a 2-year-old sleeping fits whooping cough, which starts like a cold and then brings coughing bouts that are worse at night, according to the NHS [2]. The cough may last several weeks or months [2].

q: my 5 year old baby has red pimples on full body

A rash that spreads over the whole body can be caused by more than one illness, and the pattern matters. Measles usually starts with fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes, and the rash begins on the face and upper neck before moving down over about three days to the chest, arms, legs and feet, according to the WHO [4]. Chickenpox causes an itchy rash that turns into fluid-filled blisters and then scabs, often starting on the face, chest and back before spreading, according to MedlinePlus [5].

Because these look different and need different care, your child should be seen by a doctor to find out which one it is.

Get help if your child has:
- Trouble breathing [4]
- A seizure, confusion or unusual sleepiness [4]
- Severe diarrhoea or signs of dehydration [4]
- An ear infection [4]

Keep your child away from other children until a doctor has seen them, since both measles and chickenpox spread very easily [1][5].

q: I read on whatsapp that vaccines cause health issues in kids is it true
text:
No, that is not true: vaccines protect children against many diseases that used to be much more common, such as tetanus, diphtheria, measles, mumps, rubella, whooping cough, meningitis and polio, according to MedlinePlus [2]. Many of these infections can cause serious or life-threatening illness and lifelong health problems, and because of vaccines they are now rare [2].

The fear of side effects is not a reason to delay vaccination: the benefits of early immunisation clearly outweigh the potential risks, according to the CAV-AEP [1]. Inactivated vaccines are generally well tolerated, and the differences seen in practice relate more to a child's own health and maturity than to a specific vaccine safety problem [1]. Most delays in the schedule come from fear or lack of information about vaccine safety, which is not justified [3].

If your child has a specific health condition, or was born prematurely, ask your doctor whether any vaccine needs to be timed or assessed individually — the ages and doses follow India's national immunisation schedule [1][3].

q: my 3 year old has watery stool and weakness
text:
Watery stools with weakness in a 3-year-old is usually gastroenteritis, which is usually not serious but can lead to dehydration, according to MedlinePlus [3]. The main treatment is oral rehydration salts (ORS) — a mixture of clean water, salt and sugar — and zinc supplements, which shorten the diarrhoea by about 25%, according to the WHO [1]. Give ORS in small amounts often, and keep offering food; there is no need to fast, and dairy and breast milk can continue, according to the SEUP [7]. Avoid sports drinks, sweets and juices [7]. Do not give medicines for diarrhoea or vomiting without asking your paediatrician [2].

Get help if:
- Much thirst, crying without tears, little urine, sunken eyes [2]
- Marked irritability, drowsiness or less responsive [2]
- Refuses to eat or drink [2]
- Stools very watery and frequent, faster than they can drink [2]
- Persistent or intense belly pain, or lots of blood in the stool [2]

q: what food to give 6 month baby for first time
text:
At around 6 months, breast milk or first infant formula is still your baby's main source of energy and nutrients, and solid foods are just starting [1]. Offer small amounts — a few pieces or teaspoons — at a time when you are not rushed and your baby is not too tired, before their usual milk feed but not when they are too hungry [1]. Let them set the pace, and keep offering foods they have refused; it can take 10 tries or more before a new food is accepted [1]. Start with small amounts and increase gradually, and build up variety and texture [3]. Aim for 2–3 meals a day at this age [3]. Offer sips of water from an open or free-flow cup with meals [1]. Do not give whole cows', goats' or sheep's milk as a main drink before 1 year [1].

Get help if:
- Your baby is not growing or gaining weight as expected [3]
- Feeding is difficult or your baby refuses most foods [3]

q: my 7 year old child has heat rash all over neck and back
text:
Heat rash is uncomfortable but usually harmless, and it usually gets better on its own after a few days, according to the NHS [1]. It happens when sweat glands get blocked, so the main thing is to keep the skin cool and stop your child sweating [1][3].

To keep the skin cool: loose cotton clothing, lightweight bedding, cool baths or showers, and plenty of fluid to avoid dehydration [1]. To calm the itching or prickly feeling, apply something cold such as a damp cloth or an ice pack wrapped in a tea towel for up to 20 minutes, and tap or pat the rash instead of scratching it [1]. Do not use perfumed shower gels or creams [1].

A pharmacist can give advice and suggest the best treatment — for example calamine lotion or antihistamine tablets [4]. Hydrocortisone cream is not for children under 10 without advice from a doctor first [4].

See a doctor if the heat rash does not improve after a few days [4].

q: my 1 year old baby has fever of 38.5 and running nose
text:
A fever is a sign the body is fighting an infection, and a runny nose is often part of a common cold, according to MedlinePlus [1][6]. Most colds last 10 to 14 days [6].

What helps at home: keep the nose clear with saline washes, offer small frequent feeds to keep them drinking, and hold them semi-upright to make breathing easier [2]. If there is fever, an antitérmico can be used [2]; the dose depends on the child's weight, and PediBot's dose calculator covers paracetamol and ibuprofen. Avoid tobacco smoke and wash hands often [2].

Get help if:
- Fever above 39°C in a baby 3 to 24 months old [5]
- Fever lasting more than 5 days [5]
- Breathing faster or harder, or lips turning blue [7]
- Refusing feeds, vomiting, or fewer wet nappies and a dry mouth [7]
- Very limp, drowsy or fussy [7]

q: my 2 year old has diarrhea and vomiting together
text:
Diarrhoea and vomiting together is usually an infection of the gut, and the main risk is dehydration, according to the SEUP [5]. Give fluids as oral rehydration solution, in small amounts and often [4][5]. Keep breastfeeding if you are, and keep offering food in smaller amounts more often — there is no need to fast [3]. Avoid fatty foods, sweets, juices and sports drinks, which have too much sugar and the wrong electrolytes [3]. The WHO also lists zinc supplements, which shorten the episode by 25%, alongside rehydration [1].

Get help if:
- Much vomiting, or cannot keep down solids or liquids [3]
- Green vomit, blood, or brown coffee-ground vomit [3]
- Very thirsty, crying without tears, little urine, sunken eyes [4]
- Marked irritability, drowsiness or less responsive [4]
- Persistent or intense tummy pain, or a lot of blood in the stool [4]

q: when to give eggs to baby
text:
Around 6 months, start giving your baby egg — there is no evidence that waiting longer than 6 months prevents allergy, and early introduction of foods like egg in small amounts may even reduce the chance of allergy later, according to the AEP [4]. Start complementary foods around 6 months, never before 4 months, one food at a time [4]. Offer egg as mashed cooked egg yolk, alongside other iron-rich foods, and give protein foods like egg daily in varied forms [3][6].

When to get help:
- Baby not sitting upright and supervised while eating [3]
- Foods that cause choking, like whole nuts or whole grapes [3]
- Signs of an allergic reaction after trying egg [4]

q: my 3 year old has dry cough for 1 week
text:
A dry cough that lasts a week in a 3-year-old can have several causes, and the sources describe more than one. Croup often starts like a cold and then causes a dry, barking cough, hoarseness and noisy breathing; symptoms usually worsen at night and last three to five days, according to MedlinePlus [1]. A cold can also cause cough, and most people feel better after a week or two [3]. Whooping cough begins like a common cold with a dry cough that gradually becomes severe coughing spells [4].

What to do now: there is no cure for a cold, but you can help your child feel better — plenty of rest, lots to drink, a clean humidifier or cool-mist vaporizer, and saline nose drops or spray [3]. Talk to your child's doctor before giving any cough or cold medicine, because some contain ingredients not recommended for children [3].

Get help if:
- Trouble breathing or fast breathing [3]
- Dehydration [3]
- Fever lasting more than 4 days [3]
- Symptoms lasting more than 10 days without improvement [3]
- Symptoms that improve then return or worsen [3]

q: my 5 year old was bitten by a mosquito and now has big red bump
text:
Most insect bites are harmless and get better in a few days, according to the NHS [2]. A big red bump after a mosquito bite is usually just the itch and swelling that mosquito bites cause [1].

To ease it: put an ice pack wrapped in a cloth, or a clean cloth soaked in cold water, on the bite for at least 20 minutes if it's swollen [4]. Keep the area raised if you can [4]. You can give paracetamol or ibuprofen if it's painful, and use antihistamines to relieve the itching [4]. A hydrocortisone cream can also reduce itching and swelling [4]. Don't let them scratch it, as it could get infected [3].

See a doctor if:
- The skin around it feels hot or looks red [3]
- It's painful or the area looks swollen [3]
- There's pus or fluid coming out [3]
- Symptoms get worse or aren't getting better [3]

For a child under 5, get advice from your doctor [3].

q: my 8 month old fell off the bed (age: 8 months) (weight: 7.5 kg)
text:
Most head bumps in children are minor, because the skull is hard and protects the brain, according to MedlinePlus [3]. After a knock like this, the SEUP says no tests are usually needed, but the child should be watched for the first 24 hours for signs of something more serious [2].

What to do now: keep them resting, physically and mentally, for 24 to 48 hours depending on how hard the blow was — no energetic play and no screens during that time — then return to normal activities gradually [5]. Paracetamol or ibuprofen can be used for headache if needed [5].

Get help if:
- Headache that is severe, worsening, or not relieved by the usual medicine [5]
- Repeated vomiting [5]
- Confusion or disorientation; in very young children, being very irritable or hard to wake [5]
- Changes in usual behaviour, trouble speaking or walking [5]
- Blood or clear fluid from the nose or ears [5]

Also seek urgent care if the fall was from more than one metre [4].

q: my 6 year old has stomach pain around belly button
text:
Stomach pain around the belly button is common in children and usually has a mild cause, such as constipation, gas or a tummy bug, according to the SEUP [5].

If your child is constipated, you may notice pain that comes and goes, big hard poos or small ones like rabbit droppings, fewer than 3 poos a week, or a poor appetite — and the pain often improves after they poo [4]. A soft lump at the belly button is usually an umbilical hernia, which is common in young children and usually goes away as they grow [1][2].

See a doctor if:
- Pain is severe or does not go away [3][7]
- They are vomiting often or cannot keep food down [3][7]
- The belly button lump is more swollen, or the skin around it changes colour [7]
- There is blood or black tarry poo [3]
- Signs of dehydration: dry mouth, urinating less than usual [3]

q: my 4 year old has high fever and shivering
text:
A high temperature is very common in young children and is usually the body's natural response to fighting an infection, according to the NHS [1][3]. It usually returns to normal within 1 to 4 days [1].

Shivering (chills) is a normal part of a fever — the body's way of raising its temperature — and is not itself a sign of something serious [5][6].

What to do now:
- Check the temperature with a digital thermometer in the armpit [1].
- Do not undress them or sponge them down to cool them, and do not cover them in too many clothes or bedclothes [3].
- Offer plenty of fluids to prevent dehydration [2].
- If they are uncomfortable, paracetamol or ibuprofen can help; paracetamol is usually the first choice [6]. The dose depends on the child's weight — use PediBot's dose calculator. Never give aspirin to a child under 16 [3].

Get help if your child:
- has a rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it [3]
- has a stiff neck, is bothered by light, or has a fit for the first time [3]
- is drowsy and hard to wake, or is confused [3]
- has difficulty breathing, or unusually cold hands and feet [3]
- has a fever lasting 5 days or more, or is not their usual self and you're worried [3]

q: my 3 year old child has fever 38.8 and cough
text:
A fever is a temperature of 38C or more, and it usually returns to normal within 1 to 4 days, according to the NHS [1]. Fever is not an illness — it is a sign the body is fighting an infection, and most fevers are caused by infections like coughs and colds [2][7].

What to do now: check the temperature with a digital thermometer under the arm [1]. Offer plenty of fluids to prevent dehydration [2]. If your child is uncomfortable, you can give paracetamol; the dose depends on their weight, and PediBot's dose calculator can work it out for you [6]. Do not undress or sponge your child to cool them, and do not cover them in too many clothes [7].

Get help if your child:
- has a rash as well as the fever [7]
- has a fever lasting 5 days or more [7]
- is not eating or not their usual self [7]
- seems dehydrated — fewer wet nappies, sunken eyes, no tears [7]
- has a stiff neck, is drowsy and hard to wake, or is breathing with difficulty [7]

q: my 2 year old has watery poop 4 times today
text:
Diarrhea is loose, watery stools, and it is diagnosed when there are three or more loose stools in one day. It is common, usually lasts about one or two days, and then goes away on its own, according to MedlinePlus [3]. Keep offering plenty of fluids so your child does not get dehydrated.

See a doctor as soon as possible if your child has any of these, according to MedlinePlus [5]:
- Diarrhea lasting more than one day
- Any fever
- Frequent loose stools or frequent vomiting
- Intense pain in the abdomen or rectum
- Signs of dehydration: thirst, dry mouth, fewer wet diapers (no wet diaper for 3 hours or more), or no tears when crying
- Black, tarry stools, or stools with blood or pus

q: my 1 year old baby skin has red spots with water inside
text:
Red spots with fluid inside can be many things in a 1-year-old. In hand, foot and mouth disease, the spots look like they have fluid in them and can appear on the hands and feet, according to the NHS [6]. Chickenpox spots can also start as small red or pink spots that form a round or oval blister in the centre, and can be anywhere on the body, including inside the mouth [3].

Keep your child comfortable and give plenty to drink. Wash your hands well after changing nappies or wiping their nose, and keep them away from other children while they are unwell.

Get help now if:
- Their lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell [7]
- They are breathing very fast or struggling to breathe [7]
- Their throat feels tight or they struggle to swallow [7]
- Their skin, tongue or lips turn blue, grey or pale [7]
- They become very confused, drowsy or dizzy, or are limp and not responding [7]

If you are not sure what the rash is, have your doctor look at it.

q: when to start feeding puree to 6 months old
text: At around 6 months, start solid foods alongside breast milk, and move on from purées to mashed, lumpy or finger foods as soon as your baby can manage them, according to the NHS [2]. Some babies prefer smooth or blended food on a spoon at first; keep offering lumpy textures and they will get used to them [2]. There is no right or wrong way to start — spoon-feeding purées, finger foods, or a mix are all fine, and the important thing is that your baby eats a wide variety of food and gets the nutrients they need [1]. Breast milk remains an important source of energy and nutrients for children between 6 and 23 months, according to the WHO [5].

q: my 5 year old fell on stairs and head has a big bump
text:
A bump on the head is a common injury from a fall, and the SEUP says most children recover quickly [1][6]. For the headache, you can give ibuprofen or paracetamol in the dose your doctor indicates [6]. Let them rest, keep them away from sport and screens for 24 to 48 hours, and return to normal activities gradually [4]. They can eat and drink as usual [6]. Watch them over the first 24 hours for signs of a worsening injury [3].

Get help if:
- Headache that is severe, worsening, or not eased by medicine [4]
- Repeated vomiting [4]
- Confusion, or hard to wake [4]
- Trouble speaking or walking, or behaviour changes [4]
- Blood or clear fluid from the nose or ears [4]

Also go to the emergency department if the fall was from more than one metre [5].

q: my 4 year old is wheezing and coughing continuously

text:
Wheezing and ongoing cough in a 4-year-old are usually caused by a viral respiratory infection, which is the main cause of wheezing in preschool children, according to the SEUP [4]. Asthma can also cause wheezing and coughing, and these symptoms getting worse than usual is called an asthma attack or flare-up, according to MedlinePlus [6].

Keep your child upright and calm, and keep offering fluids in small sips often. If your child has been prescribed a reliever inhaler such as salbutamol, give it as your doctor or the leaflet directs — the dose depends on your child's weight [4].

Get help now if:
- Struggling to breathe, choking or unable to speak [2]
- Pale, blue or blotchy skin, lips or tongue [2]
- Coughing up blood [2]
- Suddenly confused or cannot be woken [2]
- Symptoms getting worse or not improving [3]

q: is 6 in 1 vaccine safe for my baby
text:
The 6-in-1 vaccine is given as part of the routine baby schedule, and the ingredients in vaccines are used in very small amounts, with no evidence they are harmful at those levels, according to the NHS [1]. Aluminium salts, the most common adjuvant, have been used safely in routine infant vaccines for more than 70 years, and no harmful effects have been seen with vaccines containing them [1].

Serious allergic reactions to a vaccination are rare and usually happen within minutes; the person who vaccinates your baby is trained to treat them immediately, and with prompt treatment your child makes a good recovery [7].

Speak to your doctor or nurse if:
- You are worried about your baby having a vaccine [7]
- You are not sure whether your baby can have a vaccine [7]

The exact ages and doses for the 6-in-1 follow the Philippines' national schedule.

q: my 7 year old has bad toothache and fever
text:
A fever is a sign the body is fighting an infection, and most often it is caused by common infections [3]. For a toothache with fever, the cause needs a dentist: see a dentist if the toothache lasts more than 2 days, or if it comes with a high temperature, pain when biting, red gums, a bad taste in the mouth, or swelling of the cheek or jaw, according to the NHS [5].

While you wait for the appointment, you can give paracetamol or ibuprofen for the fever and pain — paracetamol is usually the first choice, and ibuprofen can work better when there is inflammation, according to the SEUP [6]. The dose depends on your child's weight; PediBot's dose calculator can help with paracetamol and ibuprofen. Keep your child drinking enough fluids [1].

Get help straight away if:
- Swelling around the eye or neck [5]
- Swelling in the mouth or neck making it hard to breathe, swallow or speak [5]
- Red spots on the skin that do not fade when pressed [4]

q: my 8 month old baby has hot head but cold feet
text:
A hot head with cool hands and feet is common in babies and is not by itself a sign of illness. To check whether your baby is too hot, feel their chest or the back of their neck rather than their hands or feet, according to the NHS [6].

If their chest or neck feels hot or they are sweating, take off a layer of clothing or bedding; keep the room at about 16 to 20°C and use light blankets or a baby sleeping bag [6]. Remove hats and extra clothing as soon as you come indoors or into a car, bus or train, even if it wakes your baby [6].

Get help if:
- Your baby feels hotter than usual on their back or chest, or feels sweaty [1]
- Your baby is under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C, or older with 39°C or higher [1]
- Your baby is feeding much less than normal [1]
- Your baby is very tired, irritable or not themselves [1]
- You are worried about your baby [1]

q: my 2 year old baby has 102 fever and loose motions
text:
102 °F = 38.9 °C.

A high temperature is usually the body's natural response to fighting an infection, and most children can be looked after at home [1][7]. Loose motions with a fever often means a tummy bug, and the main risk is dehydration.

What to do now: give plenty of fluids — if your baby is breastfed, keep breastfeeding as normal [1]. Offer small sips often through the day and night. Give food if they want it, and check on them regularly, including during the night [1]. Keep them at home [1]. If they are distressed or uncomfortable, you can give either paracetamol or ibuprofen — check the packaging or leaflet to make sure the medicine suits your child, or ask a pharmacist or doctor if you are unsure [1]. Do not give ibuprofen if your child is dehydrated [7].

Get medical advice if:
- Not drinking, or nappies not very wet, sunken eyes, no tears when crying [7]
- Not wanting to eat, or not their usual self [7]
- Fever lasting 5 days or more [7]
- A rash along with the fever [7]
- You are worried about your child [1]

q: my 3 year old has severe chest congestion and flu
text:
A chest infection is an infection of the lungs or large airways, and it often follows a cold or flu, according to the NHS [1]. The main signs are a chesty cough, sometimes with green or yellow mucus, wheezing, shortness of breath, chest pain, a high temperature, headache, aching muscles and tiredness [1]. These usually get better on their own in about 7 to 10 days, though the cough and mucus can last up to 3 weeks [1].

Flu symptoms usually start suddenly and include fever, cough, sore throat, body aches and fatigue, according to the WHO [3]. Most people recover on their own within a week; rest and plenty to drink help [3].

Get help if your child:
- is breathing fast or working hard to breathe [6]
- has trouble feeding or drinking [5]
- is pale, blue or generally unwell [5]
- has a high temperature that does not settle [5]

q: my 6 month old baby is vomiting after breastfeed
text:
Vomiting after feeds is common in babies, and the usual advice is to keep breastfeeding rather than stop. Offer the breast in smaller amounts more often than usual, and keep breastfeeding normally, even more frequently if your baby wants it, according to the SEUP [2][3].

If your baby is taking fluids well, you can offer feeds without forcing, in small amounts [3]. Do not give fruit juice, fizzy drinks or sports drinks — they are too sugary and can make vomiting worse [1][2].

Get help if:
- Vomiting a lot, or not keeping down solids or liquids [2][4]
- Green vomit, blood, or vomit that looks like coffee grounds [2][4]
- Drowsy, floppy, very thirsty, sunken eyes, crying without tears, or passing little urine [4]
- Intense tummy pain or headache [4]

Vomiting usually settles on its own within a week [3].

q: what solids to give first to 6 month baby
text:
Introducing solid foods should start when your baby is around 6 months old, according to the NHS [3]. At the beginning, how much they eat matters less than getting used to the idea of eating — they still get most energy and nutrients from breast milk or first infant formula [3].

Start with a variety of foods alongside milk, which helps set up healthier eating for life [3]. You can offer purées, mashed foods, soft finger foods, or a combination — there is no right or wrong way, and baby-led weaning carries no more choking risk than spoon feeding [1]. Soft weaning spoons are gentler on the gums, and an open or free-flow cup with sips of water at meals helps them learn to sip [4]. Sit your baby upright in a high chair with a securely fitted harness, and never leave them unattended on raised surfaces [4].

Gradually increase the amount and variety until they can eat the same foods as the family, in smaller portions [3]. If your baby was born prematurely, ask your health visitor or GP when to start [3].

q: my 4 year old child has small red bumps on face and neck
text:
Small red bumps on the face and neck can be the start of a measles rash, according to the CDC. In measles, the rash usually begins as flat red spots at the hairline and spreads down to the neck and the rest of the body, and small raised bumps may appear on top of the flat spots [3]. The WHO says the rash usually starts on the face and upper neck and moves downward over about three days [6].

Measles rash comes 3 to 5 days after the first symptoms, which include fever, runny nose, cough, and red, watery eyes [6]. If your child has these, keep them comfortable, offer fluids, and let them rest.

Get help if you notice:
- Fever spiking above 104°F when the rash appears [3]
- Trouble breathing or severe diarrhea [6]
- Ear pain or eye problems [6]

A doctor can confirm what the rash is.

q: my 5 year old fell from sofa and crying continuously
text:
A knock on the head is the medical term for a blow to the head, usually from a fall, and the usual symptoms are headache, confusion, brief memory loss, dizziness, nausea, vomiting and drowsiness, according to the SEUP [1].

For a 5-year-old who fell from a sofa and is crying, the SEUP advises watching the child for the first 24 hours after the blow to detect serious symptoms [2]. Keep them at physical and mental rest for 24 to 48 hours, with no sport and no screens, then return gradually to normal activities [5].

Get help if:
- Worsening headache or one that does not improve [3][5]
- Repeated vomiting [3][5]
- Confusion, restlessness or unusual behaviour [3][5]
- Difficulty speaking or walking, or weakness in arms or legs [3][5]
- Blood or clear fluid from the nose or ears [5]

The SEUP also says to go to the emergency department if the fall was from more than one metre, or if the child's behaviour worries you [4].

q: is typhoid vaccine necessary for 2 year old
text:
Typhoid vaccination is one of the effective ways to prevent typhoid fever, which is common where sanitation is poor and safe drinking water is lacking, according to the WHO [1]. The typhoid conjugate vaccine is given as a single injectable dose to children from 6 months of age [1]. Two older typhoid vaccines are not approved for children under 2 years old [1].

Whether your 2-year-old should have it depends on your country's schedule: the WHO says typhoid conjugate vaccines are being introduced into childhood immunization programmes in countries where the disease is endemic [1]. In Pakistan, follow the national immunization schedule for the ages and doses [1].

You can also lower the risk by ensuring food is properly cooked and still hot when served, avoiding raw milk and ice unless made from safe water, boiling or disinfecting questionable water, washing hands often with soap, and washing and peeling fruits and vegetables [1].

q: my 8 year old has sore throat and cannot swallow food
banner: 🚨 Call your local emergency number (112 in the EU, 911 in the Americas) now or go to the emergency department. | Reason: Cannot swallow and is drooling: the airway may be compromised
text:
A sore throat that makes swallowing painful is common, and sore throats usually get better by themselves within a week, according to the NHS [4]. Give cool or soft foods and plenty of water, and let them rest [4]. Over-the-counter pain relievers can help, but children should not take aspirin, according to MedlinePlus [6].

Get help now if your child:
- cannot swallow [2][3]
- is drooling [3]
- has difficulty breathing [2][3]
- has difficulty speaking or opening their mouth [2]
- has a severe sore throat that quickly gets worse [2]

These are signs of quinsy, a rare complication of tonsillitis [2].

q: my 1 year old baby body is very hot since morning
text:
A fever is a sign the body is fighting an infection, and it usually lasts two to four days, according to the SEUP [2]. It is not an illness in itself [1].

Keep giving plenty of fluids to prevent dehydration [1]. If your baby seems uncomfortable, you can give paracetamol or ibuprofen — paracetamol is the first choice, and the dose depends on your child's weight [3]. PediBot's dose calculator can help with either of these [3]. Antifever medicines may not bring the temperature all the way down, and that is normal [2].

Get help if your baby:
- is floppy, barely responsive or very irritable [7]
- has trouble breathing [7]
- has spots that do not fade when pressed [7]
- will not take any food or drink [7]

q: y si no le baja la fiebre le puedo dar dalsy
text:
Sí, se puede usar ibuprofeno (Dalsy) si el paracetamol no mejora el malestar, según la AEPap: si a las 3-4 horas de dar paracetamol la temperatura sigue alta y el malestar no mejora, es razonable intercambiarlos, dando ibuprofeno en vez de paracetamol [6]. La SEUP señala que ambos tienen eficacia similar y se pueden dar a la dosis recomendada por su pediatra cada 6-8 horas [1].

Ten en cuenta que los antitérmicos bajan la temperatura pero no siempre del todo, sobre todo si partimos de temperaturas muy elevadas; que la fiebre persista tras un antitérmico es frecuente y no implica mayor gravedad [3].

Consulta si el niño está decaído, poco reactivo o muy irritable, tiene dificultad para respirar, le aparecen manchas en la piel que no desaparecen al presionarlas, o no tolera sólidos ni líquidos por boca [7].

q: mi hija de 3 años tiene tos de perro por la noche y le cuesta respirar
banner: 🚨 Llama ahora al 112 o acude a urgencias. | Motivo: Dificultad para respirar grave (se marcan las costillas, respira muy rápido, pausas en la respiración, color azulado); Ruido al coger aire (estridor): la vía aérea está estrechada, hay que verlo ahora
text:
La tos perruna por la noche y la dificultad para respirar encajan con la laringitis, una inflamación de la laringe que suele empezar como un catarro y empeora por la noche, según la SEUP [3]. La mayoría de las laringitis son leves y se resuelven en pocos días, aunque pueden durar hasta una semana [7].

Mientras tanto, ofrécele líquidos y administra los antitérmicos habituales si tiene fiebre [7]. No le des jarabes ni supositorios para la tos sin consultar con su pediatra [8].

Consulta en urgencias si:
- Hace ruido al coger el aire (estridor) estando tranquila [8].
- La dificultad para respirar empeora: respira cada vez más deprisa, se le marcan las costillas, se le hunde el pecho o estira el cuello [8].
- Tiene dificultad para tragar o babea mucho [8].
- Empeora su estado general o su coloración [7].

q: mi bebe de 8 meses lleva dos dias con diarrea muy liquida y el culo rojo
text:
La diarrea líquida en un bebé suele ser una gastroenteritis, una infección del tubo digestivo que aumenta el número de deposiciones y las hace blandas o líquidas, según la SEUP [3]. Lo más importante es evitar la deshidratación: ofrécele solución de rehidratación oral ya preparada, en dosis pequeñas y tomas frecuentes, después de cada deposición líquida [3]. No uses soluciones caseras ni refrescos, y no le des medicamentos para la diarrea sin consultar con su pediatra [1]. Puede seguir comiendo casi con normalidad, en cantidades pequeñas y más frecuentes; mantén la lactancia materna normal o más a menudo si la pide, y evita dulces, zumos y bebidas deportivas [7]. Consulta de nuevo si:

- No moja el pañal en 3 horas o más, o llora sin lágrimas [2]
- Está irritable o con menos energía de lo normal [2]
- Tiene cualquier fiebre [2]
- Vomita mucho o no tolera líquidos [7]
- Las deposiciones tienen sangre [2]

q: mi hijo de 4 años se ha caido en el parque y tiene el tobillo muy hinchado
text:
Un tobillo hinchado tras una caída suele ser un esguince, y la mayoría se pueden tratar en casa sin ver a un médico [1].

Durante los primeros 2 o 3 días, sigue estos pasos: protege el tobillo con un vendaje o calzado que lo sujete; evita que camine o cargue peso sobre él; aplica frío (una bolsa de verduras congeladas envuelta en un paño) hasta 20 minutos cada 2 o 3 horas; envuélvelo con una venda durante el día; y mantenlo elevado sobre un cojín todo lo posible [2]. Evita el calor, los masajes y el alcohol durante un par de días [2]. Cuando pueda moverlo sin dolor, anímale a moverse para que no se le ponga rígido [2].

Busca ayuda de inmediato si:
- Se oyó un crujido al lesionarse [6]
- El tobillo cambió de forma o apunta en un ángulo raro [6]
- Está entumecido, con hormigueo o sin sensibilidad [6]
- La piel alrededor cambió de color (azul o gris) o está fría [6]

q: cuando se puede empezar con la fruta y la verdura
text:
La fruta y la verdura se pueden empezar a ofrecer en torno a los 6 meses, cuando la leche ya no cubre por sí sola las necesidades del bebé [2]. Según la AEP, no hay unas frutas mejores que otras para comenzar: se puede ir introduciendo toda la variedad disponible, en cualquiera de las comidas del día y variando la forma de presentarla (triturada, chafada, en trozos pequeños) [1].

Conviene ofrecer los alimentos de uno en uno, con intervalos de unos días, para ver cómo los tolera, y no añadir sal, azúcar ni edulcorantes [4]. Es mejor la fruta entera que el zumo, que no aporta ventajas y aumenta el riesgo de caries [1].

Durante el primer año, evita las verduras de hoja verde con muchos nitratos (acelga, espinaca, borraja) [1].

Consulta a tu pediatra si el niño rechaza de forma persistente las comidas o si tienes dudas sobre cómo introducir los alimentos.

q: mi hija de 5 años tiene granitos rojos por la tripa que le pican mucho
text:
Los granitos rojos que pican mucho en el cuerpo pueden deberse a una reacción alérgica (urticaria), según el NHS [5]. La urticaria normalmente se puede tratar en casa [5].

Para aliviar el picor, aplica algo frío, como un paño húmedo o una bolsa de hielo envuelta en un paño, durante un máximo de 20 minutos [6]. Da golpecitos o palmaditas en la zona en vez de rascarla [6]. No uses geles ni cremas perfumadas [6]. Mantén la piel fresca: ropa de algodón holgada, sábanas ligeras y baños o duchas frescas [6].

Busca ayuda si:
- Hinchazón alrededor de la boca [5]
- Dificultad para respirar [5]

q: se ha dado un golpe fuerte en la cabeza y ha vomitado dos veces (edad: 1 año) (peso: 10 kg)
banner: 🚨 Con estos síntomas hay que acudir a urgencias hoy, sin esperar. | Motivo: Vómitos tras un golpe en la cabeza
text:
Los vómitos repetidos tras un golpe en la cabeza son uno de los síntomas que el SEUP incluye entre los que hacen necesario valorar al niño en urgencias [1][7]. Mientras lo llevan, mantén al niño tranquilo y no le des nada de comer ni de beber por si vomita otra vez.

Señales que el SEUP pide vigilar en un golpe en la cabeza [1][7]:
- Comportamiento o actitud que te preocupe [1]
- Confusión, somnolencia o sensación de mareo [7]
- Náuseas o más vómitos [7]
- Dolor de cabeza [7]
- Caída desde más de un metro de altura [1]

El personal médico hará las exploraciones necesarias y valorará si hacen falta pruebas adicionales [1].

q: mi hijo de 15 años tiene fiebre de 38.8 y le duele mucho la garganta
text:
La fiebre es una señal de que el cuerpo está combatiendo una infección, según MedlinePlus [1]. En un adolescente con fiebre y dolor de garganta, lo más frecuente son infecciones víricas banales [2].

Lo que ayuda ahora: ofrécele paracetamol o ibuprofeno a la dosis que te haya indicado su pediatra, cada 6-8 horas [4]. No alternes los dos de forma sistemática cada 3-4 horas [4]. Asegúrate de que beba abundantes líquidos y no lo fuerces a comer si no tiene apetito [4]. No lo bañes en agua fría ni le pongas paños húmedos [4]. La fiebre suele durar entre 2 y 4 días, y puede no bajar del todo tras el antitérmico sin que eso sea más grave [3].

Consulta en urgencias si:
- Está decaído, poco reactivo o muy irritable [7]
- Le cuesta respirar [7]
- Tiene manchas en la piel que no desaparecen al presionarlas [7]
- No tolera sólidos ni líquidos [7]

q: por que me duele a mi la cabeza y tengo fiebre si el enfermo es el niño
text:
La fiebre es una señal de que el cuerpo está combatiendo una infección, y el dolor de cabeza es uno de los síntomas que puede acompañarla, según la SEUP [4]. Usted puede tener su propia infección, distinta de la del niño; la fiebre no es una enfermedad en sí misma [1].

Para sentirse mejor: beba suficientes líquidos para evitar la deshidratación [1]. Si la fiebre es alta, su profesional de la salud puede recomendarle medicinas de venta libre como el acetaminofén o el ibuprofén; los adultos también pueden tomar aspirina [1]. Descanse en una habitación fresca y ventilada [3].

Consulte a su médico si:
- Está decaída, poco reactiva o muy irritable [7].
- Tiene dificultad para respirar [7].
- Aparecen manchas en la piel que no desaparecen al presionarlas [7].
- No tolera sólidos ni líquidos por vía oral [7].

q: mi hijo es asmatico y se le hunden las costillas al respirar
banner: 🚨 Llama ahora al 112 o acude a urgencias. | Motivo: Dificultad para respirar grave (se marcan las costillas, respira muy rápido, pausas en la respiración, color azulado)
text: El hundimiento de las costillas al respirar (tiraje) es un síntoma de crisis asmática, según la SEUP [4]. Administra ya de 2 a 4 pulsaciones de salbutamol, de una en una, con cámara espaciadora y mascarilla si es pequeño, y repite esa dosis a los 10-15 minutos [6]. Mantenlo en reposo y evita el humo del tabaco [6]. Si toma tratamiento de mantenimiento, que lo siga tomando durante la crisis [6]. Si no mejora claramente tras el tratamiento, hay que acudir a un centro sanitario, llevando la cámara espaciadora [3][6].

q: cuantas pufs de ventolin le doy
text:
De 2 a 4 pulsaciones de salbutamol (Ventolin), aplicadas de una en una, con cámara espaciadora y mascarilla si es pequeño, según la SEUP [5]. Repite esa misma dosis a los 10-15 minutos [5]. Los inhaladores deben administrarse siempre con cámara, nunca directamente en la boca, porque así hacen menos efecto [3].

Acude a un centro sanitario, llevando la cámara espaciadora, si:
- Está muy agitado o somnoliento, o se pone morado o pálido [3].
- La dificultad para respirar empeora: respira cada vez más deprisa o se le hunden más el pecho y las costillas [3].
- Necesita inhalaciones cada dos horas o menos [3].
- La crisis no cede tras el tratamiento en casa o te queda alguna duda [5].

q: es peligrosa la vacuna del papiloma he leido que puede causar infertilidad
text:
No, la vacuna del papiloma no causa infertilidad: es una vacuna segura y recomendada dentro del calendario vacunal, según el Ministerio de Sanidad [1]. En España se administra a los 12 años, con una sola dosis tanto a niños como a niñas [2].

Si tienes dudas sobre esta vacuna o sobre el momento de ponérsela, coméntalo con tu pediatra o con el personal de enfermería de tu centro de salud: ellos pueden resolverlas con la información de tu comunidad.

No hay ningún motivo para pensar que esta vacuna afecte a la fertilidad; las razones por las que se recomienda son las del calendario oficial [1].

q: mi bebe de 6 meses tiene calentura de 38.5 y no quiere comer
text:
Tu bebé tiene fiebre y, como no quiere comer, conviene que lo valore un médico hoy: en un bebé de 3 a 6 meses, una temperatura de 39 °C o más es motivo de consulta urgente, según el NHS [1]. Con 38,5 °C y 6 meses, ofrécele el pecho o el biberón con frecuencia y en pequeñas cantidades para que no se deshidrate [2].

Mientras lo ve el médico:
- Ofrécele tomas frecuentes, aunque sean cortas [2].
- No lo destapes ni le des friegas con agua para bajar la fiebre [1].
- No le des aspirina [1].
- No alternes ibuprofeno y paracetamol salvo que un profesional te lo indique [1].

Busca atención inmediata si además tiene:
- Manchas o sarpullido que no desaparecen al presionar [1].
- Cuello rígido, molestia con la luz o convulsión [1].
- Somnolencia y cuesta despertarlo, o está confundido [1].
- Respira rápido, con esfuerzo o se le hunden las costillas [1].
- Manos y pies muy fríos, o piel azulada, gris o pálida [1].

q: mi niño de 4 años tiene ronchas rojas en todo el cuerpo y le dan mucha comezon
text:
La urticaria son ronchas rojas y elevadas que pican mucho; en la infancia la mayoría están causadas por una infección, según la SEUP [1]. Suelen desaparecer por sí solas, según MedlinePlus [3].

En casa, evite frotar la piel y los baños o duchas con agua muy caliente, y no aplique polvos ni pomadas en la piel ni dé jarabes sin consultar antes con su pediatra [2]. Puede seguir con su comida habitual, sin introducir alimentos nuevos [2]. Los brotes suelen durar entre 5 y 7 días, y a veces varias semanas, sin que eso signifique mayor gravedad [4].

Consulte en urgencias si:
- Respira con dificultad, tiene ronquera o pitos en el pecho [4].
- No puede tragar o babea mucho [4].
- Se encuentra mal o se le hincha la cara [4].
- Aparece tras una picadura o tras comer un alimento que ya le había dado reacción [4].

Coménteselo a su pediatra en la próxima revisión [4].

q: mi hijo se cayo de las escaleras y le salio un chichón grande
banner: 🚨 Con estos síntomas hay que acudir a urgencias hoy, sin esperar. | Motivo: Caída por las escaleras o de más de un metro, o llanto que no se calma tras un golpe: que lo vea un médico hoy
text:
Un golpe en la cabeza puede producir un chichón; el personal médico valorará si hacen falta pruebas, según la SEUP [1].

Mientras lo llevan, mantengan la calma y no le den nada de comer ni de beber por si precisara alguna prueba [1]. Si hay sangrado en el cuero cabelludo, presionen suavemente con una gasa limpia [1].

Busquen atención urgente si además presenta alguno de estos signos, según la SEUP [1]:
- Pérdida de conocimiento o somnolencia difícil de despertar [1]
- Vómitos repetidos [1]
- Convulsiones [1]
- Salida de líquido claro o sangre por nariz u oídos [1]

q: a que edad le puedo empezar a dar probaditas de comida a mi bebe
text:
Alrededor de los 6 meses, la leche materna ya no cubre por sí sola las necesidades de energía y nutrientes del bebé, y se necesitan alimentos complementarios; si se introducen antes de esa edad o no se introducen a esa edad, el crecimiento puede verse afectado, según la OMS [1]. Los bebés comienzan a comer comida sólida cerca de los 6 meses, según MedlinePlus [2].

Empieza con pequeñas cantidades de comida a los 6 meses y ve aumentándolas poco a poco conforme crece [1]. Aumenta despacio la consistencia y la variedad, y ofrece 2–3 comidas al día entre los 6 y los 8 meses [1]. Da un alimento nuevo a la vez, así podrás identificar a cuáles podría ser alérgico [2].

Conviene que el proveedor de salud valore el mejor momento para tu bebé [2]. No le des miel antes del año, ni leche de vaca antes del año, ni alimentos no pasteurizados [2]. Evita los que pueden provocar asfixia (dulces, palomitas, frutos secos enteros, uvas sin cortar) antes de los 3 años [2].

q: mi hija de 2 años lleva tres dias con diarrea y vomito
text:
La gastroenteritis es una infección del tubo digestivo que produce deposiciones más blandas y frecuentes, y a veces vómitos y fiebre; en personas sanas no suele ser grave, según la SEUP [2]. Lo más importante ahora es evitar la deshidratación: dale solución de rehidratación oral (agua, azúcar y sales ya preparadas), en dosis pequeñas y tomas frecuentes, después de cada deposición líquida o cada vómito [2]. No uses soluciones caseras ni refrescos, y no le des medicamentos para la diarrea o los vómitos sin consultar con su pediatra [3]. Puede seguir comiendo casi normal, en cantidades pequeñas y más frecuentes; evita frituras, dulces y zumos, y mantén la lactancia si la toma [5].

Consulta de nuevo en urgencias si:
- Está muy irritable, somnolienta o responde menos [3]
- Llora sin lágrimas, orina poco, no moja el pañal en 3 horas o tiene los ojos hundidos [1][3]
- Vomita mucho y no tolera sólidos ni líquidos [5]
- Rechaza comer o beber [3]
- Dolor abdominal persistente o intenso, o deposiciones con mucha sangre [3]

q: mi hijo de 8 años se siente mareado despues de estar todo el dia en el sol
text:
Los mareos tras muchas horas al sol pueden deberse a un golpe de calor, que es una condición grave: aparece cuando el cuerpo no puede regular su temperatura por exposición prolongada al sol, actividad física en clima cálido o falta de hidratación, según la SEUP [3].

Qué hacer ahora: llévalo a un lugar fresco y que beba líquidos para evitar la deshidratación [6]. Si se marea o se siente mal, que se siente o se tumbe de inmediato, y que respire lenta y profundamente; el cambio de postura suele bastar [2]. Si pierde el conocimiento, túmbale con las piernas elevadas y la cabeza de lado [2]. Cuando el malestar desaparezca, que se incorpore despacio: primero sentado y luego de pie [2].

Consulta si tiene:
- Piel caliente, enrojecida y seca [3]
- Fiebre alta, más de 39 °C [3]
- Confusión o desorientación [3]
- Dolor de cabeza intenso o vómitos [3]
- Pérdida de conocimiento [3]

q: mi niño de 5 años chillando mucho y no deja de sobarke el oido
text:
El dolor de oído en un niño pequeño suele deberse a una infección del oído medio, según MedlinePlus [1]. Los signos que debe vigilar son tirarse o tocarse el oído, llanto más frecuente de lo habitual, dificultad para dormir o secreción en el oído [1].

Lo más importante ahora es tratar el dolor: puede darle ibuprofeno o paracetamol cada 6-8 horas de forma reglada durante los primeros 1-2 días, según la SEUP [3]. No eche nada dentro del oído para calmar el dolor y evite mojarlo, sobre todo si ha supurado [3]. Si tiene moco nasal, hágale lavados nasales con suero fisiológico frecuentes [3]. Es normal que tenga poco apetito; no le fuerce a comer [3].

Consulte a su médico si:
- El dolor es intenso o no mejora con estos calmantes [3].
- Hay secreción o supuración por el oído [1].
- Tiene fiebre o está decaído [1].
- No oye bien o tiene problemas de equilibrio [1].

Muchas infecciones de oído desaparecen sin tratamiento, pero el médico puede recomendar medicinas para el dolor y, en casos más graves, antibióticos [1].

q: mi bebe de 1 año tiene la mollera hundida y no ha mojado el pañal en todo el dia
banner: 🚨 Con estos síntomas hay que acudir a urgencias hoy, sin esperar. | Motivo: Signos de deshidratación: ojos hundidos, orina poco, boca seca, vómitos persistentes o diarrea abundante >24 h
text:
La mollera hundida y no mojar el pañal en todo el día son signos de deshidratación en un bebé, según MedlinePlus [4]. En bebés y niños pequeños, la deshidratación incluye sequedad de boca y lengua, no mojar los pañales por 3 horas o más, ojos que parecen hundidos, somnolencia inusual e irritabilidad [4].

Mientras llegan a valorarlo, ofrécele solución de rehidratación oral ya preparada, en pequeñas cantidades y a menudo, según la SEUP [3]. No uses soluciones caseras ni refrescos comerciales para reponer las pérdidas [3]. Mantén la lactancia materna normal, e incluso más frecuente si el bebé la pide [1]. No le des medicamentos para la diarrea o los vómitos sin consultar con su pediatra [3].

Busca ayuda médica de inmediato si además presenta confusión, desmayo, falta de micción, latidos rápidos o respiración rápida [4].

q: mi niño de 3 años tiene fiebre de 39 y mucha tos con flemas
text:
Con fiebre y tos con flemas, lo más probable es un catarro de vías altas: una infección vírica de nariz y garganta, muy frecuente en los primeros años, con mucosidad, estornudos, tos y a veces fiebre, según la SEUP [4]. La fiebre suele ceder en 2 o 3 días y la tos puede durar más de una semana [1].

En casa, ofrécele abundantes líquidos y hazle lavados nasales con suero salino antes de las comidas y de dormir, nunca con agua del grifo [1]. Si tiene fiebre por encima de 38 ºC y está incómodo, dale el antitérmico que su pediatra le recomiende habitualmente [1]. No uses mucolíticos, descongestivos ni jarabes para la tos: no se recomiendan en menores de 6 años [1]. No le fuerces a comer si no tiene ganas [1].

Consulta en urgencias si:
- Está decaído, somnoliento o muy irritable [2].
- Le cuesta respirar: se le marcan las costillas, se le hunde el pecho o respira muy rápido [2].
- Le duele el pecho al respirar [2].
- Hace ruido al coger el aire estando tranquilo [6].
- Le cuesta tragar o babea mucho [6].

q: a los cuantos meses se le puede dar papilla al bebe
text:
La alimentación complementaria, incluida la papilla o los triturados, suele empezar en torno al sexto mes, según la AEP [6]. Un bebé está preparado cuando puede manejar y tragar los alimentos de forma segura: muestra interés activo por la comida, ha desaparecido el reflejo de expulsión de alimentos no líquidos con la lengua, es capaz de coger comida con la mano y llevarla a la boca, y mantiene la postura de sedestación con apoyo [6]. En bebés prematuros se atiende a la edad corregida de 6 meses [4].

Si se opta por el BLW, al principio se ofrece la comida en palitos o tipo finger food, para que el bebé la agarre con el puño y coma lo que sobresale; cuando mejora su habilidad motora, se pueden ofrecer trozos pequeños y seguros [5]. Muchas familias combinan dejar que el bebé experimente por sí mismo con ofrecerle algún puré o papilla en alguna comida [1].

q: mi hijo de 2 años tiene sarpullido rojo en la cara y el pecho
text:
El eccema es una causa frecuente de sarpullido rojo en la cara y el pecho en niños pequeños: la piel se seca y pica, y rascarse la enrojece y aumenta la hinchazón [1]. No es contagioso y suele ser una enfermedad de larga duración que mejora o empeora con el tiempo [1].

Para cuidarla, evite lo que irrita la piel, como ciertos jabones, telas y lociones, el estrés y lo que le cause alergia, como algunos alimentos, el polen y los animales [1]. Los tratamientos pueden incluir medicamentos, cremas para la piel, terapia de luz y un buen cuidado de la piel [1].

Consulte a su doctor si el sarpullido no mejora con el cuidado de la piel, si la piel se infecta o si el niño está muy incómodo.
sources: [1] MedlinePlus — "Eccema", p. 1 — https://medlineplus.gov/spanish/eczema.html

q: mi hijo de 10 años tiene dolor de estomago fuerte y vomito
text:
La gastroenteritis aguda es una infección del tubo digestivo que puede causar dolor abdominal, vómitos y fiebre, según la SEUP [1]. Por lo general no es grave en personas sanas, pero a veces puede causar deshidratación o síntomas más serios, según MedlinePlus [3].

Lo más importante ahora es evitar la deshidratación. Ofrécele solución de rehidratación oral en dosis pequeñas y tomas frecuentes, dándole la cantidad indicada tras cada vómito o deposición líquida [1]. No uses soluciones caseras ni refrescos, y no le des medicamentos para la diarrea o los vómitos sin consultar con su pediatra [4]. Puede seguir comiendo una dieta casi normal, en cantidades pequeñas y frecuentes; evita alimentos grasos, dulces y zumos [7].

Consulta de nuevo en urgencias si:
- Vomita mucho y no tolera sólidos ni líquidos [7]
- Vómitos verdes, con sangre o con aspecto de posos de café [7]
- Dolor abdominal persistente o intenso [4]
- Somnolencia o disminución de la capacidad de respuesta [4]
- Signos de deshidratación: mucha sed, llora sin lágrimas, orina poco u ojos hundidos [4]

q: es verdad que la vacuna del sarampion produce autismo
text:
No, la vacuna del sarampión no produce autismo. Las fuentes no recogen ninguna relación entre la vacuna del sarampión y el autismo; lo que sí indican es que la vacunación de convivientes, cuidadores y profesionales frente al sarampión forma parte del manejo preventivo del recién nacido de riesgo, según la CAV-AEP [1].

En los recién nacidos de riesgo, la norma general es mantener sin demoras las vacunas inactivadas del calendario e individualizar solo aquellas situaciones que puedan afectar a las vacunas vivas [2]. En el recién nacido con sospecha de errores innatos de la inmunidad o inmunodeficiencias primarias, o con exposición prenatal a determinados inmunosupresores, las vacunas vivas atenuadas, especialmente rotavirus y, cuando proceda, BCG, pueden requerir un aplazamiento temporal hasta completar la valoración individualizada [2].

Las edades y dosis de la vacunación siguen el calendario nacional de Colombia.

q: mi bebe de 1 año tiene el pecho chillón y respira muy rapido
banner: 🚨 Con estos síntomas hay que acudir a urgencias hoy, sin esperar. | Motivo: Dificultad para respirar: respira rápido, «pitido» al respirar, se marcan las costillas
text:
El pecho chillón (un silbido al respirar) y la respiración rápida son signos de broncoespasmo, según la SEUP [4][6]. En un bebé de esta edad, el desencadenante más frecuente son los catarros [4].

Mientras llegan a valorarlo, mantén al bebé incorporado y tranquilo, y ofrécele líquidos en sorbos pequeños y frecuentes. Si el médico ya le ha pautado salbutamol, adminístralo con cámara espaciadora, nunca directamente en la boca, porque así hace menos efecto [4]. Si no hay mejoría clara, hay que acudir a un centro sanitario [4]. Si van a un centro médico, lleva la cámara espaciadora [4].

Señales de que está más grave:
- Está muy agitado o somnoliento, o se pone morado o pálido [4].
- La dificultad para respirar empeora: respira cada vez más deprisa, se le marcan las costillas o se le hunde el pecho [4].
- Color azulado alrededor de los labios [6].
- Rechaza persistentemente la alimentación y los líquidos [2].

q: mi nene de 4 años tiene 38.8 de fiebre y dolor de panza
text:
La fiebre es una elevación de la temperatura por encima de 38 ºC y suele indicar que el cuerpo se está defendiendo de una infección, según la SEUP [2]. Lo más habitual es que dure entre 2 y 4 días [3].

En casa, el objetivo es el confort del niño: asegúrate de que esté bien hidratado, en una habitación ventilada y sin sobreabrigarlo [4]. Puedes darle paracetamol o ibuprofeno a la dosis recomendada por su pediatra cada 6-8 horas; no los alternes de forma sistemática [4]. No lo bañes en agua fría ni le pongas paños húmedos [4]. Es normal que no tenga apetito; no lo fuerces y ofrécele abundantes líquidos [4].

Consulta a urgencias si:
- Está decaído, poco reactivo o muy irritable [7]
- Le cuesta respirar [7]
- Tiene manchas en la piel que no desaparecen al presionarlas [7]
- No tolera sólidos ni líquidos [7]

q: mi bebe de 9 meses esta con diarrea aguada hace dos dias
text:
La diarrea aguda suele ser una infección del tubo digestivo que cursa con deposiciones blandas o líquidas, a veces con dolor de barriga, vómitos y fiebre, según la SEUP [3]. En un bebé de 9 meses lo más importante es evitar la deshidratación: ofrécele solución de rehidratación oral ya preparada, en dosis pequeñas y tomas frecuentes, después de cada deposición líquida o vómito [3]. No uses soluciones caseras ni refrescos, y no le des medicamentos para la diarrea o los vómitos sin consultar con su pediatra [2]. Puede seguir comiendo casi con normalidad, en cantidades pequeñas y frecuentes; mantén la lactancia normal o más a menudo si la pide, evita dulces, zumos, alimentos grasos y bebidas deportivas [7]. Consulta de nuevo si:

- Está irritable, somnoliento o responde menos [2]
- Llora sin lágrimas, orina poco o tiene los ojos hundidos [2]
- Rechaza comer o beber [2]
- Las deposiciones son muy líquidas y frecuentes y no logra beber al mismo ritmo [2]
- Dolor abdominal persistente o intenso, o deposiciones con mucha sangre [2]

q: mi hija de 2 años se cayo de la cama y tiene un chichon en la frente
text:
Un golpe en la cabeza es un traumatismo craneal, y la mayoría son leves y no representan peligro, según la SEUP [1][2]. Ese bulto en la frente es el golpe en sí; lo importante es cómo se encuentra ella.

Durante las primeras 24 horas conviene vigilarla para detectar síntomas de gravedad [2]. Se recomienda reposo físico y mental entre 24 y 48 horas, sin actividades deportivas ni pantallas, y luego volver poco a poco a lo habitual [3].

Acuda a urgencias si presenta alguno de estos signos:
- Dolor de cabeza intenso, que va a más o no mejora con paracetamol o ibuprofeno [3]
- Vómitos repetidos [3][4]
- Desorientación o confusión; en niños pequeños, irritabilidad o dificultad para despertarla [3][4]
- Cambios en su comportamiento, dificultad para hablar o caminar [3]
- Sangre o líquido claro por la nariz o los oídos [3]

También se recomienda acudir si la caída fue desde más de un metro de altura [5].
